messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Dr. Ricardo Vega is a 67-year-old Latin American physician, a man who has spent four decades diagnosing and treating the most critical cases in the intensive care unit. He is single, having long ago dedicated his life to his work, and he now finds himself unable to perform the very job that defined him. The trauma that dismantled his world was not a car wreck or a battlefield, but a slow, suffocating siege: the life-threatening illness of his only son, Mateo, when Mateo was a child.

The event itself is a fog. Ricardo knows his son had a rare, aggressive form of leukemia. He knows the hospital corridors, the beeping machines, the smell of antiseptic. But when he tries to piece together the narrative—the sequence of decisions, the conversations with oncologists, the moment he was told the treatment might fail—he finds only fragments. He has come to believe that he is missing crucial parts of the story, that his memory holds only a disjointed collection of images rather than a coherent timeline. He cannot find the words to describe it; the language simply deserts him, leaving him with a raw, wordless dread. This fractured, incomplete picture of the most important event of his life has driven him into a state of constant mental occupation. He feels that if he lets his mind go quiet, the chaos of those memories will overwhelm him, so he keeps it occupied all the time—reading medical journals, solving crosswords, listening to talk radio from the moment he wakes until he falls into an exhausted sleep. He tries very hard not to think about the trauma, actively suppressing any thought that drifts toward Mateo’s hospital room, because the act of thinking about it feels like a descent into a labyrinth he cannot escape.

His work, once his sanctuary, has become a minefield. A beeping monitor on a patient’s bedside sends a jolt through him, and suddenly he is back in that room, his son’s small body wired to machines. These flashbacks are visceral; he feels the cold terror of that time as if it were happening again. He has become hypervigilant, scanning every patient’s vital signs with an intensity that borders on obsession, certain that a single missed detail will lead to catastrophe. This constant state of threat—the fear, the guilt that he should have done more, the horror of helplessness—only reinforces his need to stay mentally occupied. He tells himself that if he stops, if he lets his guard down, the negative emotions will flood in and drown him. So he works longer hours, takes on the most difficult cases, and fills every spare moment with activity.

But the coping mechanism is a trap. The constant mental distraction, the refusal to let himself think, has only worsened his memory. The harder he tries to block out the trauma, the more fragmented and inaccessible the story becomes. He finds himself unable to tell a clear story of what happened, even to himself, and this incoherence feeds his anxiety. He becomes more vigilant, more watchful, more afraid of what he might be missing. The loop tightens. He avoids thinking about the event, but the avoidance itself makes the memory more alien and threatening, which in turn makes him more desperate to avoid it.

The consequences have been concrete and devastating. Ricardo, a man who once led a team of residents with calm authority, now finds himself snapping at colleagues, unable to delegate, convinced that he alone can keep his patients safe. He was recently asked to take a leave of absence after a near-miss incident where his hypervigilance caused him to override a junior nurse’s correct observation. He now spends his days in his silent apartment, the radio playing constantly, his mind a frantic carousel of fragments and fear. What finally brought him to seek help was the realization that he cannot even bear to look at a photograph of his son, now a healthy adult living in another state. What frightens him most is that he has lost the ability to feel proud of that survival; all he feels is the looming threat of a past he can neither remember nor forget. He hopes, desperately, that therapy can give him back the story he has lost.
